results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

results.quote: Those rules sit where a merchant meets Amazon, which answers the question the chapter opened with, which records its own systems must still track: whichever role Amazon plays,
results.finding: The callback sentence that ties the four rules to the opening question chains two 'which' clauses and a colon; both flow readers had to go back to the introduction to find 'the question' (flowA: 'the hardest sentence in the chapter'; flowB: 'chains three clauses. I had to go back to the opening paragraph'). The order is fine; the prose obscures the callback.
results.corroborated_by: reader-flowB: same takeaway sentence, had to go back to the opening paragraph to find 'the question'

results.quote: managed databases (run by a provider rather than by the team using them) that its own teams could run, and Fulfillment by Amazon, its warehouse service for other sellers, letting their items carry the delivery promise of Prime, Amazon's paid membership with fast shipping
results.finding: The thesis paragraph packs three inline glosses (managed databases, FBA, Prime) and four rules into two long sentences; flowA read it twice, flowB stopped at 'run by a provider' next to 'teams could run'. Split the paragraph or move the glosses out.
results.corroborated_by: reader-flowB: the 'managed databases (run by a provider ...) that its own teams could run' clash in the same paragraph

results.draft_locus: Teams, Ownership and the Contract as the Only Door ¶1-¶2
results.quote: Of its three well-known team rules, one is in Amazon's own documentation, one in a digest of its CTO's interview, and the third only in a former engineer's recollection.
results.finding: flowA: the next paragraph puts two rules (two-pizza, you build it you run it) in one block headed only 'Two-pizza teams', so the reader has to go back to match each rule to its source; 'its CTO' is the only hint that Vogels is the CTO.

results.draft_locus: Teams, Ownership and the Contract as the Only Door ¶4
results.quote: Ten years later, in his 2016 retrospective on AWS, he wrote that the lesson of building management APIs first was one "we had already learned from our experiences with Amazon retail".
results.finding: flowA: a forward reference to Fulfillment by Amazon in the middle of the team-rules section, and the 2016 'management APIs first' quote does not clearly connect to the mandate it is meant to confirm.

results.draft_locus: Other Shops, Other Agents: 2022 to 2026 ¶3-¶5 and Figure 5
results.quote: imports merchants' catalogs into its own surface (Shop Direct, Buy for Me)
results.finding: flowA: the text runs Buy with Prime, Shop Direct, Rufus, Buy for Me, while Figure 5 and the inference callout group Shop Direct with Buy for Me as imports, with Rufus (Amazon's own agent) between them; the reader had to regroup the products. The declared paragraph order (also not strictly chronological: Shop Direct 2025 before Rufus 2024) is the source of the difficulty.

results.draft_locus: The Promise Is the Product, inference callout after ¶6
results.quote: because orders placed after 21:00 are picked the next morning
results.finding: flowB: the 21:00 pick cut-off right after the 'ordered before 22:00' rule reads as a possible contradiction; the box never says outright that the mismatch is the point. (flowA separately found the curated-subset sentence tacked on at the end of the same box.)

Andy Jassy is never introduced as Amazon's CEO; a reader new to commerce cannot tell whose letter this is (Bezos is named elsewhere, Vogels only as 'its CTO'). All does_not_know terms are otherwise defined at or just after first use.
results.corroborated_by: reader-flowA: 'Jassy's 2024 shareholder letter: Jassy is never introduced.'

results.draft_locus: KEY POINTS bullet 1; Teams ¶3; inference callout after 2001 ¶5
results.quote: The transferable rule is the one that made the split survivable: every team exposes its data only through a service interface, and nobody reads another team's database.
results.finding: The reader gets the wall-first sequence, the 100-150 services at the 99.9th percentile, the scale gap, the contract rule for vendors and scripts and operability, but misses two expected points: that the 'API mandate' is only a 2011 recollection, not an Amazon document, and that a merchant whose product page is assembled from several systems meets the aggregation and tail-latency problem in miniature. The draft has both (Teams ¶3 and Where the Evidence Stops; the inference callout after the wall section), but the KEY POINTS bullet presents the no-direct-reads rule as Amazon's without the provenance caveat, and the aggregation point sits only in a callout.
